passages.t: A spear and a water jug in Saul's camp
passages.happening:
The Ziphites come to Saul again and tell him that David is hiding on the hill of Hachilah. Saul goes down with three thousand chosen men to search for him (verses 1-2). David sends out spies and learns where Saul has camped. Saul is lying in the inner circle of the camp, with Abner and the army around him (verses 3-5).

David asks who will go down with him into the camp, and Abishai says he will (verse 6). That night they find Saul asleep, ‘with his spear stuck in the ground by his head’ (verse 7).

Abishai says, “Today God has delivered your enemy into your hand. Now, therefore, please let me thrust the spear through him into the ground with one stroke. I will not need to strike him twice!” (verse 8).

David will not allow it: “Do not destroy him, for who can lift a hand against the LORD’s anointed and be guiltless?” (verse 9). ‘As surely as the LORD lives, the LORD Himself will strike him down; either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish’ (verse 10). They take the spear and the water jug by Saul's head and go. No one wakes, ‘because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This is the second time David has Saul in his power and lets him go. In chapter 24 the chance fell into his lap in a cave. This time David goes looking for it, and walks into the middle of Saul's army at night.

The setting is again the Wilderness of Ziph, the rough country southeast of Hebron toward the Dead Sea, where the people of Ziph had already once given David away. Saul's three thousand chosen men are a standing force, and Abner, his commander, is his cousin.

Two of David's men are named. Ahimelech the Hittite shows that David's band included foreigners. Abishai son of Zeruiah is David's nephew, and with his brothers Joab and Asahel he will be a fierce and often ruthless presence through David's reign.

Saul's spear, stuck upright by his head, marks where the king sleeps. It is almost his scepter. It is also the spear he threw at David, twice, and at his own son Jonathan. David takes it, saying without words that he could have used it, and did not. The water jug was precious in the desert, and taking it proves how close he came.

The deep sleep is the same word used for the sleep God brought on Adam and on Abram. It means that the sleeping camp is not luck. God has put Saul into David's hand, and David still will not strike.

David has learned the lesson of Nabal. The LORD deals with those who wrong him, in his own time.
passages.later:
The same deep sleep came on Adam: ‘So the LORD God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep’ (Genesis 2:21), and on Abram at the covenant: ‘Abram fell into a deep sleep’ (Genesis 15:12).

Chronicles names Abishai's family: ‘the three sons of Zeruiah were Abishai, Joab, and Asahel’ (1 Chronicles 2:16).
passages.asks: Abishai said one stroke would do it, and David said no. Ask who in your life urges you to settle things by force, and whether you listen. And ask whether you can trust God to deal with someone in his own time, without your help.

passages.t: A last plea, and a parting
passages.happening:
David crosses to the other side and stands on a hilltop far off (verse 13). He shouts to Abner. Is he not a man? Who in Israel is his equal? ‘Why then did you not protect your lord the king when one of the people came to destroy him?’ (verse 15). Abner deserves to die for not guarding the LORD's anointed. ‘Now look around. Where are the king’s spear and water jug that were by his head?’ (verse 16).

Saul knows the voice. “Is that your voice, David my son?” “It is my voice, my lord and king,” David said (verse 17). Why is the king chasing him? What has he done (verse 18)? If the LORD has stirred Saul up against him, may the LORD accept an offering. But if people have done it, they have driven him out of his share in the LORD's inheritance (verse 19). He asks Saul not to let his blood fall far from the presence of the LORD. The king of Israel has come out to look for a flea, ‘like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains’ (verse 20).

Saul answers, “I have sinned. Come back, David my son. I will never harm you again, because today you considered my life precious. I have played the fool and have committed a grave error!” (verse 21).

David tells him to send a young man for the spear (verse 22). ‘May the LORD repay every man for his righteousness and faithfulness’ (verse 23). As he valued Saul's life, may the LORD value his (verse 24). Saul says that David will do great things and will surely prevail. ‘So David went on his way, and Saul returned home’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The chapter deliberately repeats chapter 24. Saul pursues with three thousand men, a companion urges David to kill him, David refuses because Saul is the LORD's anointed, takes a token as proof, calls out from a distance, and Saul confesses and calls him ‘my son’. The differences sharpen the lesson. This time David takes the first step, the token is a weapon and not a scrap of robe, and David does not even have to fight his own conscience.

There is irony in David's taunt. He scolds the general for failing to guard the LORD's anointed, which is exactly what David himself has been doing.

David's plea speaks of being driven from the LORD's inheritance. The LORD was worshiped in his own land and among his own people. To be hunted out of Israel was to be pushed toward the gods of other lands. David is not saying that the LORD is limited to one country. He is saying that being driven from God's people cuts him off from worshiping God among them. His exile is a loss of the soul as well as a danger to the body.

A partridge was a bird hunted on foot until it tired. The picture mocks the king of Israel spending his army on one fugitive.

Saul's ‘I have played the fool’ recalls Samuel's first rebuke, that Saul had acted foolishly (13:13). His words are true. But there is no lasting change. He goes home, and David still has to flee. This is the last time they meet. David will never see Saul again.
passages.later:
A psalm of the sons of Korah gives words to the same longing: “My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?” (Psalm 42:2).

When Saul died, David did not rejoice. He sang, “Saul and Jonathan, beloved and delightful in life, were not divided in death” (2 Samuel 1:23).
passages.asks: Saul said, ‘I have sinned’, and went home unchanged. Ask whether your words of sorrow have ever outrun any change in your life. And ask what it means to value someone's life, as David valued Saul's, when they have not valued yours.
